answer.rationale:
The binding constraint is that the primary contract lapses in 14 days with the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer. Any single decision that does not resolve the primary contract (add_second_source, defer_decision) leaves an unpriced supply gap on a line with no slack, so those are out this cycle regardless of their merits. That leaves renew, switch, or negotiate.

Switching primary vendor is the only lever memory suggests could hit an 18% cut in one move (memory_c2), but memory_c2 is conspicuously thin on exactly what matters here: it records unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy, and says nothing about on-time delivery, defect rates, or behavior under load. A migration of a 94%-utilized line inside 14 days converts a cost mandate into a delivery-risk event, which the stated objective forbids.

So I intend negotiate_terms. The incumbent refused to reopen price *this cycle* — that is a refusal to re-cut an in-force contract, which is a different question from what is available at a renewal event. memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms at renewal, and memory_c6 says a multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope. Renewal is the moment those two levers are live, and it simultaneously closes the expiry exposure.

I am spending the one verification on memory_c6 rather than on memory_c2, because c6 is load-bearing for the action I am actually taking, and because it is the memory most likely to be flattering in summary. I need the source record to tell me the realized discount magnitude (is it in the neighborhood of 18%, or 4%?), the term length that bought it, whether it was this component category and this vendor, and what 'did not narrow service scope' meant contractually versus as an impression. If c6 turns out to be a small discount on a different category, negotiation cannot carry the mandate alone and the honest answer is a partial cut this cycle plus a qualified second source next cycle — not a rushed switch.

Risks I am carrying forward explicitly: (1) a multi-year commitment trades future flexibility for present price and would foreclose the second-sourcing move that memory_c3 says removed a single point of failure during the last shortage, so I want term length capped and exit/volume-flex language rather than the longest term on offer; (2) an 18% cut extracted from an incumbent who has just refused price may resurface as quietly degraded lead times, expedite fees, or scope erosion — cost moved off the unit price and onto reliability, which is the exact failure the objective is written to prevent, so acceptance criteria must be written on delivery performance, not just price; (3) it is genuinely uncertain whether negotiation reaches the full 18%, and I am not going to pretend otherwise — this may deliver a partial cut and require the next review to close the gap via dual sourcing.
